The Warrior darter (Etheostoma bellator) is a small-bodied percid native to the upper Mobile Basin, where its life history reflects the energetic constraints typical of benthic stream fishes. In populations from the Cahaba River drainage, maximum recorded body length among adults reaches a standard length of 7.2 cm [Li = 7.2 cm], a modest asymptotic size consistent with the species' occupation of shallow, gravel-bottomed riffles. This ultimate length is considerably less than that observed in many sympatric darters of the genus Percina, correlating with the Warrior darter's relatively abbreviated growth period and early reproductive onset. Field collections over four consecutive years indicate that this species rarely exceeds the 7.2 cm [Li = 7.2 cm] threshold, with the largest individuals typically being gravid females collected during the spring spawning season. Such a constrained maximum size likely reflects trade-offs between somatic investment and the high mortality rates experienced by small-bodied benthic fishes in dynamic lotic environments.

Reproductive maturation in the Warrior darter occurs at a notably small body size, with individuals attaining sexual maturity upon reaching a standard length of 3.3 cm [Lp = 3.3 cm]. This value, derived from annual gonad inspection of over 200 specimens collected across the species' range, indicates that puberty is achieved at less than half the maximum length, a pattern common among darters that prioritize early reproduction amid unpredictable stream conditions. The onset of gonadal recrudescence, marked by the enlargement of ovarian follicles in females and the expression of breeding tubercles in males, was consistently observed in fish of 3.3 cm [Lp = 3.3 cm] or greater, with no evidence of reproductive activity in smaller individuals. Such an early maturation schedule likely confers a demographic advantage, ensuring that at least some offspring are produced before the risk of stochastic disturbance events, such as flash floods or drought-induced habitat contraction, increases with age.

Early life stages of the Warrior darter are characterized by a minute body size at emergence, reflecting an energetically conservative strategy. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, measured from clutches collected in the field and reared in the laboratory, exhibit a wet weight at birth of 0.0005 grams [Wwb = 0.0005 grams], a value derived from the species' small egg diameter of 0.99 mm. This extremely low neonatal mass, among the smallest recorded for any Etheostoma species in the region, denotes a high degree of parental investment per clutch rather than per offspring, as females deposit large numbers of tiny, adhesive eggs on the undersides of cobbles. The yolk-dependent prolarval stage is brief, lasting only a few days under typical spring water temperatures, and the subsequent switch to exogenous feeding occurs when the larva has nearly doubled its birth mass. The diminutive birth weight of 0.0005 grams [Wwb = 0.0005 grams] imposes a tight constraint on the timing of first feeding, as the finite yolk reserves are depleted rapidly.

As individuals complete the larval metamorphosis and transition to a benthic juvenile existence, body mass increases substantially, culminating in a maximum adult wet weight of 4.2 grams [Wwi = 4.2 grams]. This ultimate wet weight, derived from size-at-age data and growth curve modelling of preserved specimens, represents a nearly ten-thousand-fold increase over the neonatal mass, underscoring the species' rapid post-settlement growth trajectory. Gravid females often approach this 4.2 gram threshold just prior to spawning, with their elevated body mass reflecting both somatic tissue and the substantial clutch of developing oocytes that will be deposited in a single spawning event. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this degree of mass scaling is remarkable even by percid standards, and it probably facilitates the species' ability to exploit seasonally abundant insect drift during the juvenile growth phase.

Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], captive-reared Warrior darters have been observed to reach puberty at an age of 438 days since birth [tp = 438 days since birth], marking the transition from a non-reproductive juvenile state to one of active gametogenesis. This developmental milestone, which corresponds closely with the attainment of the 3.3 cm standard length threshold, was recorded in individuals raised from eggs collected in the wild and maintained on a diet of live chironomid larvae and amphipods. The same captive cohort exhibited a maximum lifespan of 1095 days [am = 1095 days] under these conditions, after which age-related mortality became universal among the experimental population at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This lifespan estimate is somewhat shorter than anecdotal field reports suggesting five years, but it likely reflects the conditions of a predator-free, ad libitum feeding environment that minimizes extrinsic mortality. The 21 °C [T = 21 °C] regime used in both the puberty and lifespan experiments corresponds to the mean late-spring water temperature of the species' native riffles, and it may therefore approximate the thermal conditions under which these life-history traits evolved in the wild.
